paras: The Harlem police clubbing of August 1905 took place on August 8, 1905, near One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street in Harlem, New York City, when police reserves clubbed a crowd of Black people after a policeman was attacked while arresting a Black woman. Three people were arrested and held in the Harlem Court for participating in a riot. The only report found, in the New York Evening World, presented the incident as a "race riot" started by the woman.

According to the Evening World, Policeman John Elliott of the East One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street station was slashed with a razor and beaten into unconsciousness while attempting to arrest a Black woman. The paper did not say what the woman was accused of or who wielded the razor. Reserves under Sergeant Lake were sent from the station and, on arriving, found Elliott on the pavement with three policemen standing over him and holding back a Black crowd with night sticks.

The reserves then charged into the crowd and, in the paper's words, "clubbed about them savagely until their arms were tired." They also drew their revolvers and threatened to shoot the first Black person who showed a weapon. Once the crowd was dispersed, ambulances were called and surgeons dressed the wounds and cuts, though the number of injured was not given.

Three prisoners, whose names and race the paper did not give, were taken to the East One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street station and later arraigned in the Harlem Court, where they were held for participating in a riot. Elliott was taken home after his injuries were dressed. No report of a later trial, of the woman's fate, or of any inquiry into the police clubbing was found.

The Evening World ran the story on page 3 under the headline "Virago Starts a Race Riot in Harlem," with the subhead "Scalps Cracked by Reserves When Policeman Elliott Was Attacked by a Mob." Its account came entirely from the police side: it called the crowd "a mob of negroes," blamed the woman for the outbreak, and described the reserves' clubbing without criticism. No version from the woman, the crowd or the prisoners appeared, and no other white or Black newspaper was found to have carried the incident.

accounts.label: Police account (as printed by the Evening World)
accounts.gist: Elliott was attacked by a Black crowd while arresting a Black woman; reserves found him on the pavement with three policemen holding off the crowd, clubbed the crowd until it dispersed, and arrested three people who were held for riot.

framing.detail: The Evening World headlined 'VIRAGO STARTS A RACE RIOT IN HARLEM' and described, without criticism, reserves who 'clubbed about them savagely until their arms were tired', with no account from the crowd.

record_check.dossier: Correct that no one is named; the targets were an uncounted Black crowd.

record_check.record: three Black people were held for riot
record_check.dossier: The article says 'three prisoners' were held for participating in a riot; it does not state their race.
Unnumbered injuries: surgeons treated 'wounds and cuts' and the headline speaks of cracked scalps; a count cannot be given.
One policeman (Elliott) injured; the paper does not state his race.
Police reserves of the East 126th Street station under Sergt. Lake.
Clubbing with night sticks; revolvers drawn with a threat to shoot.

info: 1905-08-08 (reported as 'to-day' in the evening paper of that date)
Near One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street, Harlem, New York City
An unnamed and uncounted crowd of Black people ('a mob of negroes') clubbed by police reserves; no names given
The crowd was said to have attacked Policeman John Elliott, who was slashed with a razor and beaten unconscious while trying to arrest a Black woman; the charge against the woman is not stated
Police reserves of the East One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Street station under Sergt. Lake, plus three policemen already at the scene
The three prisoners were arraigned in the Harlem Court and held for participating in a riot; no later disposition was found
